High blood pressure (BP) is largely attributable to the risk of developing cardiovascular diseases (CVDs),1 which is an important cause of death in this era. Controlling BP is one of the essential risk modifications of CVDs. Several studies suggested that respiratory muscle training (RMT) lowers BP.2 Inspiratory muscle training (IMT) is a physical training that uses the diaphragm and accessory respiratory muscles to repeatedly inhale against resistance. Recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) showed that IMT, especially high-intensity IMT, can reduce BP.3-4

A recent systematic review focused on RCTs regarding the effectiveness of RMT in patients with hypertension,5 in which load RMT may have a better effect on BP than unload RMT. However, this review was very heterogeneous due to the inclusion of the different types of respiratory training protocols applied. In addition, no clear benefit of the intervention on 24-hour BP, which is more closely associated with the incidence of CVDs,6-7 could be established Furthermore, because they did not use the GRADE approach, the uncertainty of each evidence is still unclear.5 In this study, we focused on the efficacy of high-intensity IMT, and aimed to investigate the available literature and determine whether high-intensity IMT improves 24-hour BP in patients with above-normal BP.
P: Patients with above-normal BP
I: IMT with load (any level of load)
C: Any kind of respiratory training with no load or with lower load than that of intervention group
Primary: Ambulatory (24-hour) BP, all adverse events; Secondary: Casual BP, adherence of IMT

We used a systematic review protocol template(dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.biqrkdv6). We followed the Preferred reporting items for systematic review and meta-analysis 2020 (PRISMA-2020) for preparing this protocol.8 We will publish this protocol in protocols.io (https://www.protocols.io/).
3.2 Inclusion criteria of the articles for the review
3.2.1 Type of studies

We will include randomized controlled trials that assessed the effects of IMT on BP and reported before and after ambulatory BP (mean 24-hour, daytime, and nighttime systolic and diastolic BP) in IMT and control groups. We will not apply language or country restrictions. We will include all papers including published, unpublished articles, abstract of conference and letter.
We will exclude crossover trials, cluster-randomized, quasi-randomized and non-randomized trials. We will not exclude studies based on the observation period or publication year.
3.2.2 Study participants
The inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis were as follows:
Participants were adults (age ≥18 years) with above-normal hypertension, which is generally defined as systolic BP ≥120 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥80 mmHg, or under antihypertensive medication
Studies combined with other types of physical interventions (e.g. aerobic exercise and/or hypocaloric diet) or non-pharmacological therapy will be excluded.
Studied that had mixed interventions (e.g. IMT combined with breathing exercises) will be excluded.
Studies that reported data from only one training session will be excluded.
All identified articles were assessed independently by 2 reviewers (YK and NS), and disagreements were resolved by discussion.
Duration/Frequency: No criteria were set on the duration or frequency of IMT.
Intensity: No criteria were set on the intensity of IMT.
Sham respiratory training
No-load respiratory training
Respiratory training with lower load than that of intervention group
3.3.1 Primary outcomes
1. Twenty-four hours ambulatory systolic BP (daytime and nighttime)
Definition: The systolic BP with ambulatory BP monitoring with mean 24-hour, daytime, and nighttime systolic BP
Period: evaluated within 2 months post-intervention
2. Twenty-four hours ambulatory diastolic BP (daytime and nighttime)
Definition: The diastolic BP with ambulatory BP monitoring with mean 24-hour, daytime, and nighttime diastolic BP
Period: evaluated within 2 months post-intervention
3. All adverse events
Definition: Incidence proportion of all adverse events. Definitions of adverse events are set by original authors.
Period: evaluated during follow up period
3.3.2 Secondary outcomes
1. Systolic casual BP
Definition: The systolic BP (continuous) measured by any standard devices, such as electronic or traditional mercury sphygmomanometer
Period: evaluated within 2 months post-intervention
2. Diastolic casual BP
Definition: The diastolic BP (continuous) measured by any standard devices, such as electronic or traditional mercury sphygmomanometer
Period: evaluated within 2 months post-intervention
Definition: The percentage of completed training sessions per prescribed training sessions.
Period: evaluated throughout the intervention

3.5 Data collection and analysis
3.5.1 Selection of the studies

Two independent reviewers (YK and NS) will screen titles and abstracts, followed by the assessment of the eligibility based on the full texts. We will contact original authors if relevant data is missing. Disagreements between the two reviewers will be resolved by discussion, and if this fails, a third reviewer will act as an arbiter (KM).
3.5.2 Data extraction and management
Two reviewers (YK and NS) will perform independent data extraction of the included studies using standardized data collection form. We will use a pre-checked form using 10 randomly selected studies.

The form will include the information on study design, study population, interventions (including the intensity, duration, and frequency of IMT), and outcomes (24 hours ambulatory systolic and diastolic BP). Any disagreements will be resolved by discussion, and if this fails, a third reviewer will act as an arbiter (KM).
3.6 Assessment of risk of bias in included studies

Two reviewers (YK and NS) will evaluate the risk of bias independently using the Risk of Bias 2.9 Disagreements between the two reviewers will be discussed, and if this fails, a third reviewer (KM) will be acting as an arbiter, if necessary.
3.7 Measures of treatment effects
We will pool the relative risk ratios and the 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the following binary variables:

We will pool the mean differences and the 95% CIs for the following continuous variables: 24 hours ambulatory systolic and diastolic BP, the incidence rate of all adverse events, systolic and diastolic casual BP, and the percentage of completed training sessions per prescribed training sessions.
3.8 Unit of analysis issues
All intervention groups that are relevant to this review will be included.
3.9 Handling of missing data
We will ask not-presented data to the original authors.
3.9.1 Missing outcomes
We will perform the intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis for all dichotomous data as much as possible.
For continuous data, we will not impute missing data based on the recommendation by Cochrane handbook.10 We will perform meta-analysis about the available data in the original study.
3.9.2 Missing statistics

When original studies only report standard error or p-value, we will calculate the standard deviation based on the method by Altman.11 If we don't know these values when we contact the authors, standard deviation will be calculated by confidence interval and t-value based on the method by Cochrane handbook10, or validated method.12 Validity of these methods will be analyzed by sensitivity analysis.
3.10 Assessment of heterogeneity

We will evaluate the statistical heterogeneity by visual inspection of the forest plots and calculating the I2 statistic (I2 values of 0% to 40%: might not be important; 30%to 60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity; 50% to 90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity; 75% to 100%: considerable heterogeneity). When there is substantial heterogeneity (I2> 50%), we will assess the reason of the heterogeneity. Cochrane Chi2test (Q-test) will be performed for I2 statistic, and P value less than 0.10 will be defined as statistically significant.
3.11 Assessment of reporting bias

We will search the clinical trial registry system (ClinicalTrials.gov and ICTRP) and will perform extensive literature search for unpublished trials. To assess outcome reporting bias, we will compare the outcomes defined in trial protocols with the outcomes reported in the publications. We will assess the potential publication bias by visual inspection of the funnel plot. We will conduct Egger test to assess the publication bias. We will not conduct the test when we find less than 10 trials or trials which have similar sample size. We will also assess the potential publication bias by visual inspection of the funnel plot.
Meta-analysis will be performed using Review Manager software (RevMan 5.4.2). We will use a random-effects model.
3.13 Subgroup analysis
To elucidate the influence of effect modifiers on results, we will evaluate the subgroup analyses of the primary outcomes on the following factors when sufficient data are available.
(For intervention) Exercise intensity (Maximal inspiratory pressure [PImax] <30% 30% ≤PImax), Duration of the IMT (≥8 weeks, <8 weeks), Weekly exercise time (min/week) (< 75 vs 75≤)
3.14 Sensitivity analysis
We will undertake the following sensitivity analyses for the primary outcomes to assess whether the results of the review are robust to the decisions made during the review process.
Exclusion of studies using imputed statistics.
Exclusion of studies with high or some concern in the overall assessment of ROB.
4. Summary of findings table

Two reviewers (YK and KM) will evaluate the certainty of evidence based on the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach.13 Disagreements between the two reviewers will be discussed, and if this fails, a third reviewer (ST) will be acting as an arbiter, if necessary. will be acting as an arbiter, if necessary.
Summary of findings table will be made for the following outcome based on the Cochrane handbook.10
24 hours ambulatory systolic BP
24 hours ambulatory diastolic BP
